verdicts.trueWording: handwritten on vellum with a quill pen
verdicts.note: georgerrmartin.com 25 Apr 2018, raw HTML fetched 200. Full sentence: "I've seen the archmaester's manuscript. Since it was handwritten on vellum with a quill pen, he required my help in transcribing the text to a more modern format: WordStar 4.0, on a DOS computer." Quote exact; the transcription conceit (Gyldayn wrote it, Martin transcribed) and its joking frame are both explicit on the page, which also ends "Archmaester Gyldayn is hanging up his quill for a while."

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: advances by chronology rather than by scene — the excerpt renders full dramatised scenes with dialogue
verdicts.trueWording: plans were laid in 58 AC for Jaehaerys and Alysanne
verdicts.note: Quote "plans were laid in 58 AC" is verbatim (once, mid-sentence, not as a sentence opener despite the feature label 'regnal-year sentence openers'). 58 AC is the only regnal year in the entire excerpt; later transitions are relative ('A few days later', 'After taking leave of White Harbor', 'The longer the queen stayed'). The second limb fails: the excerpt descends into extended scenes at Winterfell built from direct dialogue (Alaric Stark's "I hope you brought something warmer than that", the exchange at the Wall), which the sibling claim 364 itself asserts.

verdicts.trueWording: Theomore Manderly is reported to have said
verdicts.note: Both hedges are verbatim on the page: "'I had not known there were so many smallfolk in the city,' Theomore Manderly is reported to have said" and "Her first sight of the Wall from above took Alysanne's breath away, Her Grace would later tell the king." Both mediate speech through testimony. Scope note only (not a failed limb): the excerpt also carries much unhedged direct dialogue, so the hedging is a recurring device rather than a universal one.

verdicts.trueWording: His Grace; Her Grace; Lord Stark; whilst; mayhaps; amongst
verdicts.note: "His Grace" x3, "the queen" x21, "Lord Stark" x2 all verbatim; archaic diction present as 'whilst' x4, 'amongst' x2, 'mayhaps', 'elsewise', 'needs must'-register throughout. Colloquial flourishes are on the page too: Lord Manderly's fool — "Methinks Lord Alaric has not moved his bowels since he was twelve" — and Alaric's "That's good. Fewer would be even better." Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: rivals drove them from their rich lands along the Mander
verdicts.note: Claim carries no quote, so graded on substance. Direct speech is substantial and embedded: Manderly, Alaric Stark, Lord Commander Burley and the queen all speak in quotation marks inside the chronicle narration. Family history compressed into a single sentence is present twice — House Manderly ("Having originated in the Reach centuries before, they had found refuge near the mouth of the White Knife when rivals drove them from their rich lands along the Mander.") and Lady Stark ("She was a Mormont of Bear Isle... took an axe to a pack of wolves when she was twelve, killed two of them, and sewed a cloak from their skins.").

verdicts.trueWording: I love reading popular histories myself, and that's what I was aiming for here
verdicts.note: georgerrmartin.com/fireandblood/ raw fetch 200. Martin, quoted in the publisher announcement: "I do want to stress... that FIRE & BLOOD is not a novel... let's call this one 'imaginary history' instead. The essential point being the 'history' part. I love reading popular histories myself, and that's what I was aiming for here..." Quote exact (curly apostrophe on page); both limbs supported.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: Martin says it makes sense he would not have all the information — that sentence is the Winter Is Coming writer's own gloss, not a Martin quote
verdicts.trueWording: it is all possible answers, not meant to be definitive
verdicts.note:
Quote "he wouldn't have all the information" is verbatim on the page, but I checked the raw HTML: it sits in the article's own

body paragraph ("Fire & Blood is 'written' by Archmaester Gyldayn of the Citadel, so it makes sense that he wouldn't have all the information."), authored by Dan Selcke — NOT inside the adjacent

carrying Martin's words. The second limb IS Martin verbatim in that blockquote: "in the case of things like Valyria and the dragon eggs, it is all possible answers, not meant to be definitive." So the mysteries limb verifies and the attribution limb does not.

verdicts.trueWording: Being A History of the Causes, Origins, Battles, and Betrayals
verdicts.note: reactormag.com raw fetch 200. Masthead reads: "THE PRINCESS AND THE QUEEN, OR, THE BLACKS AND THE GREENS / Being A History of the Causes, Origins, Battles, and Betrayals of that Most Tragic Bloodletting Known as the Dance of the Dragons, as set down by Archmaester Gyldayn of the Citadel of Oldtown ((here transcribed by GEORGE R.R. MARTIN))". Long descriptive title and transcription credit both present; the 'Being A History of...' formula is squarely early-modern.

verdicts.trueWording: so we must dance along with the rest
verdicts.note: First body paragraph in full does exactly this: "To characterize the dark, turbulent, bloody doings of this period as a 'dance' strikes us as grotesquely inappropriate... 'The Dying of the Dragons' would be altogether more fitting, but tradition and time have burned the more poetic usage into the pages of history, so we must dance along with the rest." Objection plus deference to tradition, both in the opening paragraph.

verdicts.trueWording: the conflict burst into the open on the third day of third moon
verdicts.note: No quote supplied, graded on substance; the count checks out exactly. Four abstract paragraphs precede any scene: (1) the name and the 129-131 AC span, (2) "There were two principal claimants to the Iron Throne" — claimants, (3) "The Dance split the Seven Kingdoms in two" — scale and consequences (Targaryen power diminished, dragons reduced), (4) "The Dance was a war unlike any other" — character of the war. The fifth paragraph descends to the dated day: "Long simmering, the conflict burst into the open on the third day of third moon of 129 AC...". Minor slack: paragraph 1 is about the war's name, so the four listed topics map mainly onto paragraphs 2-4.

verdicts.trueWording: with knives and lies and poison; lords, knights, and smallfolk
verdicts.note: Both parenthesised exemplars are verbatim: "as lords, knights, and smallfolk declared for one side or the other" and "a war fought in shadows and stairwells, council chambers and castle yards with knives and lies and poison." Further triads and and-chains on the same page: "tooth and claw and flame", "the kith, kin, and children", "stealth, murder, and betrayal", "the dark, turbulent, bloody doings". Every limb supported.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: without heavy Latinate vocabulary — the excerpt's opening sentence is "the savage internecine struggle for the Iron Throne"
verdicts.trueWording: at the hour of the bat; a general alarum; a moon's turn
verdicts.note: All four archaic markers verify verbatim: "whilst"/"Whilst", "without raising a general alarum", "for a fortnight or a moon's turn", "at the hour of the bat" and "It was the hour of the owl." The negative limb is the failure: the same excerpt reaches for markedly Latinate diction — "savage internecine struggle", "strikes us as grotesquely inappropriate", "two principal claimants", "became embroiled" — so the page does not support 'without heavy Latinate vocabulary' as stated.

verdicts.trueWording: thereafter it became the custom to refer to "greens" and "blacks"
verdicts.note: No quote supplied, graded on substance. The asterisk hangs on "Queen Alicent and her party, the so-called greens, *" and the footnote reads: "* In 111 AC, a great tourney was held at King's Landing on the fifth anniversary of the king's marriage to Queen Alicent. At the opening feast, the queen wore a green gown, whilst the princess dressed dramatically in Targaryen red and black. Note was taken, and thereafter it became the custom to refer to 'greens' and 'blacks'..." Asterisked footnote, tourney origin, both colour-names glossed — every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: No doubt the phrase originated with some singer.
verdicts.note: Quote exact, including the full stop, in the opening paragraph, immediately after the chronicler calls 'dance' "grotesquely inappropriate" and immediately before he proposes the soberer "The Dying of the Dragons" and concedes to "the more poetic usage". The romance-to-song / sobriety-to-record contrast is therefore explicit in context; scope note only, the page shows this move once rather than establishing a repeated 'habit'.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the named hour dates the discovery of the body, not the death — "His body was discovered by a serving man at the hour of the bat"
verdicts.trueWording: on the third day of third moon of 129 AC
verdicts.note: "third day of third moon" is verbatim, in "the conflict burst into the open on the third day of third moon of 129 AC, when the ailing, bedridden King Viserys I Targaryen closed his eyes for a nap in the Red Keep of King's Landing, and died without waking." Day, moon and year all present. But the page attaches no hour to the death itself: the hour of the bat marks the serving man's discovery of the body, and "It was the hour of the owl" marks the summoning of the small council. The calendar-precision reading holds; the specific limb dating the death to a named hour does not.
